verse.text: The elder, to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth.
verse.note: The writer gives a title and no name. The word can mean simply an older man or the holder of a recognized leadership role in a community; here it works as a title the recipient would know. Early tradition identifies the writer with John, but the letter itself does not say so, and scholars disagree about his identity.

verse.text: Beloved, I pray that you may do well in every respect and be in good health, just as your soul is doing well.

note.term: do well in every respect and be in good health

verse.note: A wish for the recipient’s health and well-being was a standard opening in ancient letters, and this is that convention. The verb, traditionally “prosper,” means for things to go well in general and does not specifically refer to wealth. The same verb is repeated of Gaius’s soul, which the translation keeps with “do well … is doing well.”

verse.text: For I rejoiced greatly when brothers came and testified to your truth—how you are walking in truth.
I have no greater joy than this: to hear that my children are walking in the truth.
Beloved, you act faithfully in whatever you do for the brothers, strangers though they are.
They have testified to your love before the assembly. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God,
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “church,” which is near-universal and familiar. A first-century hearer knew this word as the ordinary term for a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament’s word for Israel assembled. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution, so this translation uses “assembly” throughout, though the word can sound like a single meeting where an ongoing community is meant.

The verb is more than saying goodbye. In the period it regularly meant equipping travelers for the next stage of a journey with food, money, or companions. Gaius is being asked to provide for these traveling workers materially.

verse.text: for they set out for the sake of the Name, taking nothing from the Gentiles.
verse.note: The Greek says simply “the name,” with no further qualifier. Most interpreters take it to mean the name of Jesus, as in similar expressions in Acts, though Jewish usage also spoke of “the Name” as a reverent way of referring to God. Some translations supply “his” or “Christ’s.”

The word literally means people of the nations, that is, non-Jews. Since many believers were themselves non-Jews, here it means outsiders to the believing community, and some versions translate “pagans” or “unbelievers.” The point is that these travelers took no support from those they were trying to reach, so fellow believers needed to provide it.

verse.text: So we ought to take in such people, so that we may become fellow workers with the truth.
verse.note: The Greek can mean either working alongside the truth, with truth pictured as an active partner, or working together with the travelers on behalf of the truth. This translation takes the first reading, which fits verse 12, where the truth itself is said to testify. Many versions take the second.

verse.text: I wrote something to the assembly, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, does not welcome us.
verse.note: The same verb in verse 10 means refusing hospitality to the traveling brothers. Here, where the elder is not physically present, it may mean that Diotrephes refuses to recognize the elder’s authority or to accept what he wrote, and some versions translate it that way. The earlier letter mentioned here has not survived, unless it is one of the other letters of John, which is uncertain.

verse.text: For this reason, if I come, I will bring up the things he is doing, babbling against us with malicious words. And not content with that, he not only refuses to welcome the brothers himself but also stops those who want to and throws them out of the assembly.
Beloved, do not imitate what is evil but what is good. The one who does good is from God; the one who does evil has not seen God.
Everyone has testified in Demetrius’s favor, and so has the truth itself. We also testify, and you know that our testimony is true.
I had many things to write to you, but I do not want to write to you with ink and pen;
rather, I hope to see you soon, and we will speak face to face.
Peace to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends by name.
verse.note: Some English Bibles, including the King James Version, count this closing greeting as part of verse 14, giving the letter fourteen verses. Modern Greek editions and most recent translations number it as verse 15. The wording is the same either way.
